    Abstract
    The Super High Momentum Spectrometer (SHMS) has been built for Hall C at the Thomas Jefferson National Accel-
    erator Facility (Jefferson Laboratory). With a momentum capability reaching 11 GeV/c, the SHMS provides measure-
    ments of secondary charged particles produced in electron scattering experiments using the maximum available beam
    energy from the upgraded Jefferson Lab accelerator. The SHMS is an ion-optics magnetic spectrometer comprised of
    a series of new superconducting magnets which transport charged particles through an array of triggering, tracking,
    and particle-identification detectors that measure momentum, energy, angle and position in order to allow kinematic
    reconstruction of the events back to their origin at the scattering target. The detector system is protected from back-
    ground radiation by a sophisticated shielding enclosure. The entire spectrometer is mounted on a rotating support
    structure which allows measurements to be taken with a large acceptance over laboratory scattering angles from 5.5◦
    to 40◦ , thus allowing a wide range of low cross-section experiments to be conducted. These will complement and
    extend the previous Hall C research program to higher energies.
    Keywords: Magnetic spectrometer, Electron scattering, Tracking detectors, Particle identification, Electron
    calorimetry, Radiation shielding.

659      The incoming neutron flux also has two components.
660   Neutrons from excited nuclei will typically not exceed
661   10 MeV. The other neutrons are produced through di-
662   rect interactions with only one nucleon in the nucleus.
663   These will have high energies, but the flux is low. As
664   shown by the MCNP calculation, which has reliable low
665   energy neutron cross sections, 0.5 m of concrete almost
666   fully thermalizes 1 MeV neutrons. Thus, 2 m of con-
667   crete should be sufficient to thermalize the first com-
668   ponent. Some of these will be captured in the con-
669   crete, but to eliminate the surviving thermal neutrons
670   a layer of boron is needed. There are two relevant reac-
671   tion channels: (n, γ) and (n, αγ). The former produces
672   high energy photons, but the cross section is relatively
673   small. The latter produces a 0.48 MeV photon for every
674   captured neutron. The thermal cross section is about
675   10 kbarn, and even at 1 MeV it is still in the barn range.
676   The majority of neutrons can thus be expected to be cap-
677   tured in a sufficiently thick boron layer. An optimal
678   shielding configuration would also stop these photons
679   produced in the capture. At 0.48 MeV, the photoelectric
680   effect and Compton scattering contribute about equally
681   to the attenuation in lead. Photons from the latter will
682   also need to be absorbed.
683      Thus, placing the lead in front of the boron layer has          Figure 22: Photograph of the SHMS beam-side shield wall in cross-
684   limited benefit. It will not affect the neutron flux, but          section view, showing the layers of different materials making up the
                                                                         wall.
685   will create an additional source of photons. The more
686   lead one places after the boron, the more efficiently
687   these photons will be suppressed. From the point of

1654   3.9.8. Calorimeter Calibration
1655      The ability of particle identification of a calorimeter
1656   is based on differences in the energy deposition from
1657   different types of projectiles. The deposited energy is
1658   obtained by converting the recorded ADC channel value
1659   of each module into an equivalent energy.
1660      The data analysis procedure corrects for the gain
1661   differences in the process of calorimeter calibration.
1662   Good electron events are selected by utilising the gas
1663   Cherenkov detector(s). The standard calibration algo-
1664   rithm [63] is based on minimization of the variance of
1665   the estimated energy with respect to the calibration con-
1666   stants, subject to the constraint that the estimate is un-
1667   biased (relative to the primary energy). The momentum
1668   of the primary electron is obtained from the tracking in            Figure 43: An electron sample (selected through Cherenkov PID) in
                                                                           the calorimeter before calibration. The peak of the E Norm distribution
1669   the magnetic field of the spectrometer.                             is clearly greater than 1 and is relatively wide.
          The deposited energy per channel is estimated by

                             ei = ci × Ai ,                 (11)

1670   where i is the channel number, ci is the calibration con-
1671   stant, Ai is the FADC pulse integral signal. Note that
1672   the Preshower signals are corrected for the light atten-
1673   uation dependence versus horizontal hit coordinate y.
1674   The calorimeter calibration can be checked by compar-
1675   ing the track momentum to the energy deposition in the
1676   calorimeter. The ratio -

1678   electrons, E Norm should be equal to 1 as all energy

                                                                           1749      All trigger-related PMT signals from both the SHMS
